cultivar: Cangwu and Liubao population bushes (medium-leaf) and Guangxi large-leaf cultivars
processing: Post-fermented: spread, fixed at low temperature, rolled and pile-fermented with added water for days to weeks (the factory 'cold-water piling' developed at Wuzhou in 1958), dried, then steamed, packed into large bamboo baskets and aged in warehouses, usually for a year or more before sale.
harvest_season: Spring and summer pickings; the grade (Te Ji, then 1 to 6) tracks leaf size and tenderness rather than season, and late-autumn 'frost' leaf goes into Lao Cha Po.
appearance_dry: Dark brown-black, even, lightly glossy twisted leaves, sometimes with specks of yellow 'golden flower' mould in older baskets.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-amber to ruby-brown, clear and bright.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark reddish-brown leaves, even in colour and without any green.
taste_profile: Smooth, sweet and woody with the classic betel-nut note, dried jujube and a cooling, faintly medicinal finish; thick but never bitter.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice for a few seconds with boiling water, then short steeps; the spent leaves can be simmered for a last pot. A clay pot suits it, and it is good brewed strong in a thermos.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing or batch year and by factory – Wuzhou Tea Factory (Three Cranes), Wuzhou Zhongcha and Maosheng are the big names, each with batch numbers – and by grade. Market lots run from 1–3 years (still a little piley) through 5–10 years, the value sweet spot, to 15–20+ years sold as aged tea. Farmhouse 'nong jia' Liu Bao without piling is a separate line that ages like sheng.
description:
Liu Bao is the dark tea of Guangxi, from the hills around Wuzhou near the Guangdong border and named after Liubao, a township in Cangwu County where it was first made. It is the southern cousin of ripe pu-erh and of Hunan's bricks, and the thing that marks it out is a flavour the Chinese call betel-nut aroma, a sweet, woody, faintly medicinal note prized in good lots. Its history is a trading one: it was shipped down the river to Guangzhou and on to Southeast Asia, and the usual story says it was the tea of Malaysia's tin mines.

Modern Liu Bao is made in factories by a method developed at Wuzhou from 1958: the leaf is fixed and rolled, then piled with added water for days or weeks so microbes do the darkening (a gentler, shorter version of the ripe pu-erh pile), dried, steamed and packed into big bamboo baskets, which go into warehouses to age. The Wuzhou factories' ageing cellars are part of the tea's reputation, and the baskets breathe, which is why basket-aged tea tastes cleaner than tea sealed in a brick. There is no smoke and much less earthiness than in ripe pu-erh.

Brewed hot after two rinses it opens woody and jujube-sweet, finds its betel-nut note by the third or fourth steep and keeps going for ten, ending cool and faintly herbal; simmering the spent leaves gives one more thick pot. The mistakes are cool water, skipping the rinse and using too little leaf: it wants heat and weight. It takes food well and is popular with Cantonese drinkers.

It is sold by year, factory, batch number and grade, loose from baskets or repacked into small baskets, tins and boxes. Young factory tea can carry a damp 'pile' smell that fades with a few years; five to ten years is where price and pleasure meet, and genuinely aged lots cost accordingly. Taste for sweetness and a clean finish, and walk away from anything sour or musty. Farmhouse 'nong jia' Liu Bao, made without piling, is a different, greener tea that ages slowly and is sold under the same name.

If ripe pu-erh feels too heavy, Liu Bao is the lighter, cleaner dark tea to try, and a basket of a mid-aged grade is one of the cheapest ways to own an ageing tea.
sources_note: No English Wikipedia article for Liu Bao tea exists at time of writing ('Liubao tea' / 'Liupao tea' are missing; 'Liu Bao' is a historical person). Dating of the factory cold-water piling method to the 1950s–60s follows Chinese trade histories; exact years vary.
history:
Liu Bao takes its name from Liubao in Cangwu County near Wuzhou, Guangxi, where it began before spreading to more than twenty counties. Its old route has its own name, the Tea Boat Road: from the Hekou wharf in Liubao by river to the Xi River and Guangzhou, then on to Hong Kong, Macau and Southeast Asia. That is why it is known as a tea of the overseas Chinese.

The modern tea dates from the state factory era. The Wuzhou factory dates from the 1950s and, by one press account, developed cold-water piling in 1958, a controlled wet pile. Exports reached 117 tons in 1962. In Hong Kong it was called 'Guangxi old tea', and sales of such old tea there ran to about 4,000 tons a year in the 1990s.

Today it is a Chinese geographical indication product and national intangible heritage, and Guangxi passed a dedicated regulation on the industry in November 2025.
